meta.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin); high-dose vs low-dose intensification of the same statin to lower LDL-C below 100 mg/dL
meta.indication: secondary prevention of major cardiovascular events in stable, clinically evident coronary heart disease with LDL-C <130 mg/dL on atorvastatin 10 mg

n_randomized.quote: A total of 10,001 patients underwent randomization and received double-blind treatment with either 10 mg or 80 mg of atorvastatin.
n_randomized.note: 10,003 underwent randomization, 2 not given study drug (Fig. 1: 5006 assigned 10 mg, 4995 assigned 80 mg). Original target enrollment ~8600 (registry S3 enrollment count 8600).

median_followup.quote: Patients were followed for a median of 4.9 years.
median_followup.note: 4.9 years converted to months (4.9 x 12). Design paper S4 expected an average of 5 years.

primary_endpoint.value: Time to first major cardiovascular event: death from CHD, nonfatal non-procedure-related myocardial infarction, resuscitation after cardiac arrest, or fatal or nonfatal stroke
primary_endpoint.quote: The primary end point was the occurrence of a first major cardiovascular event, defined as death from CHD, nonfatal non–procedure-related myocardial infarction, resuscitation after cardiac arrest, or fatal or nonfatal stroke.
primary_endpoint.note: Endpoint change during the trial: 'In February 2003, the steering committee added stroke (fatal or nonfatal) to the primary efficacy outcome.' The paper states this was made before any data were reviewed. The original primary outcome (major coronary event) is reported as a secondary: HR 0.80 (0.69-0.92), P=0.002 (Table 2).

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Men and women aged 35-75 with clinically evident CHD (prior MI, angina with objective evidence of atherosclerotic CHD, or prior coronary revascularization); after washout, LDL-C 130-250 mg/dL and TG <=600 mg/dL to enter 8-week open-label atorvastatin 10 mg run-in; randomized only if mean LDL-C <130 mg/dL at end of run-in
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: Eligible patients were men and women 35 to 75 years of age who had clinically evident CHD, defined by one or more of the following: previous myocardial infarction, previous or current angina with objective evidence of atherosclerotic CHD, and a history of coronary revascularization.
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Run-in rule (Methods, Study Protocol): 'patients with LDL cholesterol levels between 130 and 250 mg per deciliter (3.4 and 6.5 mmol per liter, respectively) and triglyceride levels of 600 mg per deciliter (6.8 mmol per liter) or less entered an eight-week run-in period of open-label treatment with 10 mg of atorvastatin per day.' Randomized if 'mean LDL cholesterol level of less than 130 mg per deciliter'.

planned_events.quote: This modification led to an increase in the projected number of primary events to 950 (750 coronary events plus 200 strokes) during the trial, providing the study with a statistical power of 85 percent to detect an absolute reduction of 17 percent in the five-year cumulative rate of the primary efficacy outcome in the group given 80 mg of atorvastatin, as compared with the group given 10 mg of atorvastatin, with the use of a two-sided test at an alpha level of 0.05.
planned_events.note: Original plan: ~8600 patients and 750 major coronary events over an average of 5.5 years; increased to 950 when stroke was added in Feb 2003. Observed primary events 434+548=982.

assumed_rrr.quote: providing the study with a statistical power of 85 percent to detect an absolute reduction of 17 percent in the five-year cumulative rate of the primary efficacy outcome
assumed_rrr.note: The paper words it as an 'absolute reduction of 17 percent in the five-year cumulative rate'; this reads as a 17% proportional reduction of the rate (a 17-point absolute difference is implausible at ~10% event rates). Recorded as RRR 0.17; see open_questions. Earlier epidemiologic expectation in the same section: '20 to 30 percent fewer recurrent coronary events at five years'.

power.quote: providing the study with a statistical power of 85 percent
power.note: Power for all-cause death: 'The study had a statistical power of only 40 percent to detect a 10 percent reduction in the risk of death from any cause'.

alpha.quote: For the final primary analysis, an adjusted P value of 0.049 was considered to indicate statistical significance, given a type I error rate of 0.05.
alpha.note: Two interim efficacy analyses with a two-sided Peto boundary; nominal final alpha 0.049 two-sided.

stopped_early.quote: Two interim efficacy analyses were performed and were based on a two-sided Peto type of monitoring boundary.
stopped_early.note: Not stopped early; ran to planned completion (registry S3 completion 2004-08; data as of January 29, 2005). Not stated in a single sentence; inferred from the full report.

baseline.unit: mg/dL (mean, at randomization after 10 mg run-in)
baseline.note: 98 +/- 18 mg/dL in the 10 mg group, 97 +/- 18 in the 80 mg group (~2.5 mmol/L; CTT S6 Table 1 lists TNT baseline LDL-C 2.52 mmol/L). Pre-run-in: 'from a mean of 152 mg per deciliter (3.9 mmol per liter) to a mean of 98 mg per deciliter (2.6 mmol per liter)' (35% reduction during open-label 10 mg).
NOT FOUND: apoB not reported in the main paper.
NOT FOUND: not reported. Difference of means TC 175 - HDL-C 47 = 128 mg/dL would be a derived estimate only.
NOT FOUND: not reported in the main paper.

biomarker_effects.method: LDL-C method not stated in the main paper
biomarker_effects.quote: Mean LDL cholesterol levels during the study were 77 mg per deciliter (2.0 mmol per liter) among patients receiving 80 mg of atorvastatin and 101 mg per deciliter (2.6 mmol per liter) among those receiving 10 mg of atorvastatin (Fig. 2A).
biomarker_effects.note: Active comparator, not placebo: 'placebo_adjusted' here means the between-arm difference (80 mg minus 10 mg). Both values DERIVED from the reported arm means: -24 mg/dL = 77 - 101; -23.8% = -24/101. The paper reports no between-arm percentage or confidence interval.

biomarker_effects.method: CTT individual-participant data; LDL-C difference at 1 year
biomarker_effects.location: CTT 2010, Table 1 (columns: n, comparison, mean follow-up in survivors (years), baseline LDL-C (mmol/L), LDL-C difference at 1 year (mmol/L))
biomarker_effects.note: Between-arm (80 mg vs 10 mg) LDL-C difference at 1 year = -0.62 mmol/L, read from CTT full text (Europe PMC XML of PMC2988224). Consistent with S1 arm means 77 vs 101 mg/dL (24 mg/dL x 0.02586 = 0.62 mmol/L). change_pct copied from the derived S1 row. CTT check (derived, not from a source): 0.78^0.62 = 0.86 expected RR vs observed HR 0.78.

biomarker_effects.quote: Total cholesterol levels (Fig. 2B) and triglyceride levels (Fig. 2C) decreased significantly from baseline to week 12 in the group given 80 mg of atorvastatin (P<0.001 for both comparisons), and the levels remained stable during the treatment period.
biomarker_effects.note: NOT FOUND as a number: shown only in Fig. 2C (not digitized). Quote reconstructed across a two-column page break of the PDF.

biomarker_effects.quote: Both doses of atorvastatin produced nonsignificant increases over baseline in high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels, with no significant difference between the groups during the course of the study (Fig. 2D).
biomarker_effects.note: No significant between-arm difference; number not given (Fig. 2D). Quote joins 'nonsig-' / 'nificant' across a page break.

biomarker_effects.quote: During the open-label period, the LDL cholesterol level was reduced by 35 percent in the overall patient population, from a mean of 152 mg per deciliter (3.9 mmol per liter) to a mean of 98 mg per deciliter (2.6 mmol per liter).
biomarker_effects.note: Not a between-arm effect: within-patient change on atorvastatin 10 mg vs off-statin screening; context only, do not use as the randomized contrast. -54 mg/dL derived (98-152). Quote joined across a column break.

biomarker_effects.quote: Plasma LDL cholesterol reductions from baseline were dose related, with 25% to 61% reduction from the minimum dose to the maximum dose of 80 mg atorvastatin once a day.
biomarker_effects.note: Phase 2 dose-response (n=81, placebo arm included) published 1995, before readout. Change from baseline, not placebo-subtracted (placebo_adjusted=null). 10 mg value not stated in abstract; CURVES (Am J Cardiol 1998, PMID 9514454, abstract read) gives atorvastatin 10 mg -38%, so the 10 vs 80 mg gap was expected to be roughly 20+ percentage points.

hr.unit: hazard ratio (primary end point, 80 mg vs 10 mg)
hr.quote: A primary event occurred in 434 patients (8.7 percent) receiving 80 mg of atorvastatin, as compared with 548 patients (10.9 percent) receiving 10 mg of atorvastatin, representing an absolute reduction in the rate of major cardiovascular events of 2.2 percent and a 22 percent relative reduction in risk (hazard ratio, 0.78; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.69 to 0.89; P<0.001).
hr.note: Table 2: CHD death HR 0.80 (0.61-1.03), P=0.09; nonfatal non-procedure MI 0.78 (0.66-0.93); stroke 0.75 (0.59-0.96), P=0.02; major coronary event (original primary) 0.80 (0.69-0.92); hospitalization for CHF 0.74 (0.59-0.94); death from any cause 1.01 (0.85-1.19), P=0.92. Pfizer topline S2: '22 percent fewer cardiovascular events'.

ci_low.quote: hazard ratio, 0.78; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.69 to 0.89

ci_high.quote: hazard ratio, 0.78; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.69 to 0.89

p.quote: hazard ratio, 0.78; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.69 to 0.89; P<0.001
p.note: Below the adjusted final significance threshold of 0.049.

events_treatment.quote: A primary event occurred in 434 patients (8.7 percent) receiving 80 mg of atorvastatin

events_control.quote: as compared with 548 patients (10.9 percent) receiving 10 mg of atorvastatin
events_control.note: 10 mg arm N=5006 (active control, not placebo). Total first primary events 982 (above the 950 projected). Including subsequent events: 545 vs 715 major cardiovascular events.

safety_signals.value: Persistent ALT/AST elevations >3x ULN: 60 (1.2%) with 80 mg vs 9 (0.2%) with 10 mg, P<0.001
safety_signals.quote: The incidence of persistent elevations in liver aminotransferase levels was 0.2 percent in the group given 10 mg of atorvastatin and 1.2 percent in the group given 80 mg of atorvastatin (P<0.001).
safety_signals.note: Named in the abstract conclusion: 'This occurred with a greater incidence of elevated aminotransferase levels.' Pfizer topline S2: 'The incidence of liver enzyme elevations in both groups was within existing product labeling.'

safety_signals.value: Treatment-related adverse events 406 (8.1%) vs 289 (5.8%); discontinuation for treatment-related AEs 7.2% vs 5.3% (both P<0.001)
safety_signals.quote: Adverse events related to treatment occurred in 406 patients in the group given 80 mg of atorvastatin, as compared with 289 patients in the group given 10 mg of atorvastatin (8.1 percent vs. 5.8 percent, P<0.001). The respective rates of discontinuation due to treatment-related adverse events were 7.2 percent and 5.3 percent (P<0.001).
safety_signals.note: Sentences reconstructed from a two-column PDF layout; wording verbatim.

safety_signals.value: No excess myalgia or rhabdomyolysis: treatment-related myalgia 4.8% vs 4.7% (P=0.72); 5 rhabdomyolysis cases (2 on 80 mg, 3 on 10 mg); no persistent CK elevations
safety_signals.quote: Treatment-related myalgia was reported by 241 patients in the group given 80 mg of atorvastatin and by 234 patients in the group given 10 mg of atorvastatin (4.8 percent and 4.7 percent, respectively; P=0.72).
safety_signals.note: Table 3 footnote: none of the rhabdomyolysis cases were believed to be related to the study drug.

safety_signals.value: No mortality benefit and a nonsignificant excess of noncardiovascular deaths: 158 (3.2%) vs 127 (2.5%), HR 1.25 (0.99-1.57), P=0.06; all-cause death 284 vs 282, HR 1.01 (0.85-1.19)
safety_signals.quote: There were 127 deaths from noncardiovascular causes in the group given 10 mg of atorvastatin (2.5 percent) and 158 in the group given 80 mg of atorvastatin (3.2 percent; hazard ratio, 1.25; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.99 to 1.57; P=0.06).
safety_signals.note: Authors: no single cause or cancer type accounted for it; cancer deaths 85 vs 75 (HR 1.13, P=0.42). CV deaths 126 vs 155 (HR 0.80, P=0.08). Not confirmed later: CTT 2010 (S6) found 'No significant effects were observed on deaths due to cancer or other non-vascular causes' across 26 trials.

safety_signals.value: No excess hemorrhagic stroke: 16 (80 mg) vs 17 (10 mg)
safety_signals.quote: There were 16 hemorrhagic strokes in the group given 80 mg of atorvastatin and 17 in the group given 10 mg of atorvastatin.

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: HMGCR (statin target) LDL-lowering variants protect against cardiovascular events, with the same effect per unit LDL-C as PCSK9 variants
genetics.effect: OR 0.81 (0.72-0.90) per 10 mg/dL lower LDL-C for the HMGCR score
genetics.quote: Variants in PCSK9 and HMGCR were associated with nearly identical protective effects on the risk of cardiovascular events per decrease of 10 mg per deciliter (0.26 mmol per liter) in the LDL cholesterol level: odds ratio for cardiovascular events, 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 0.89) for PCSK9 and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.72 to 0.90) for HMGCR.

genetics.finding: HMGCR variants lower LDL-C and slightly raise type 2 diabetes risk and body weight, mirroring the statin diabetes signal (an on-target effect)
genetics.effect: 0.06 mmol/L lower LDL-C per rs17238484-G allele; T2D OR 1.02 (1.00-1.05) per allele; intensive vs moderate statin trials T2D OR 1.12 (1.04-1.22)
genetics.quote: The increased risk of type 2 diabetes noted with statins is at least partially explained by HMGCR inhibition.

genetics.finding: LDL-C is causal; CTT meta-analysis: more vs less intensive statin regimens (including TNT) reduce major vascular events by 15% for a 0.51 mmol/L further reduction, the same per-mmol/L effect as statin vs control (RR 0.78 per 1.0 mmol/L overall)
genetics.quote: similar proportional reductions in major vascular events per 1·0 mmol/L LDL cholesterol reduction were found in all types of patient studied (rate ratio [RR] 0·78, 95% CI 0·76-0·80; p<0·0001), including those with LDL cholesterol lower than 2 mmol/L on the less intensive or control regimen.

consensus_explanation.summary: TNT showed that raising atorvastatin from 10 to 80 mg in stable CHD lowered mean on-treatment LDL-C from 101 to 77 mg/dL (about 0.62 mmol/L more) and cut first major cardiovascular events by 22% (434 vs 548 events; HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.69-0.89, P<0.001 over a median 4.9 years), with consistent reductions in nonfatal MI and stroke. The investigators concluded that the LDL-C/CHD-risk relationship of earlier statin trials holds even at very low LDL-C. Later meta-analyses that included TNT (Cannon 2006; CTT 2010) found that intensive statin therapy reduces mainly nonfatal events and gives the same benefit per mmol/L as statin vs control, which made the 'lower is better' case for a target (HMGCR) and biomarker (LDL-C) that genetics also supports. The caveats, all stated by the authors, were: no difference in all-cause mortality (the trial had only 40% power for it), a borderline excess of noncardiovascular deaths (HR 1.25, P=0.06) that CTT later did not confirm across trials, and more persistent transaminase elevations (1.2% vs 0.2%) and treatment-related discontinuations on 80 mg.

Registry record (S3 first posted 2006-05-18; no results posted)

open_questions: Comparator: TNT compares 80 mg with 10 mg atorvastatin, so all 'placebo-adjusted' effects are between-arm differences against an active statin. The calculator should treat -0.62 mmol/L as the incremental LDL-C contrast.

Between-arm LDL-C percentage (-23.8%) and absolute difference (-24 mg/dL) are derived from the reported arm means (77 vs 101 mg/dL); the paper gives no between-arm estimate or CI. CTT Table 1 gives -0.62 mmol/L at 1 year.
Assumed effect wording: the paper says '85 percent to detect an absolute reduction of 17 percent in the five-year cumulative rate'. Recorded as RRR 0.17.
The primary endpoint was changed mid-trial (stroke added Feb 2003, before unblinding per the authors); the original primary (major coronary event) was also significant (HR 0.80, 0.69-0.92).
Triglyceride and HDL-C between-arm changes are shown only in figures; numbers not captured. apoB, non-HDL-C and Lp(a) were not reported in the main paper.
Pitt editorial (S5) not read beyond its opening paragraph (paywalled), so its view is not used.
CTT check (derived): 0.78^0.62 = 0.86 expected RR vs observed HR 0.78 (CI 0.69-0.89 includes 0.86). TNT's mean follow-up (5.0 y) is similar to CTT trials.
Registry NCT00327691 was first posted in 2006, after the readout, and has no posted results.
